channel.title: Deseret News - Faith
channel.description: Faith news and stories from Deseret News

item.title: An Idaho pioneer town welcomes public to new Montpelier temple
item.description: Montpelier, Idaho, a town of fewer than 3,000 residents settled along the Oregon Trail more than 160 years ago, held a Sept. 8 media day for its new Latter-day Saint temple ahead of an Oct. 18, 2026 dedication. Elder Mark D. Eddy, a General Authority Seventy and assistant executive director of the Church's Temple Department, said the building honors the area's pioneer heritage and will serve about 15,000 local members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The report was published by Church News, a Deseret-affiliated publication, which pointed readers to TheChurchNews.com for its full coverage.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: President Uchtdorf salutes training missionaries for ‘Here am I, send me’ willingness
item.description: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, acting president of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, addressed missionaries at an evening devotional at the Provo Missionary Training Center on Tuesday, Sept. 8, alongside his wife, Sister Harriet Uchtdorf. According to Church News, Uchtdorf praised the missionaries for choosing to serve, quoting Isaiah 6:8's declaration "Here am I; send me" as an example of exercising agency. He also paraphrased a line from the "Harry Potter" book series, telling missionaries that "it is your choices, not just your abilities, which show who you truly are." The devotional also touched on themes of invitations, goal-setting, faith and enduring in service without growing weary, per Church News' report.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Conspiracy thinking can undermine faith | Opinion
item.description: In a Deseret News opinion piece, faith and perspective writer Jacob Hess examines how immersion in conspiracy-theory thinking can erode religious faith rather than simply harming mental health, drawing on the experience of Utahn Kris Kofoed, who stepped back from alternative-media podcasts after feeling they were taking over his thinking. Pontifical University of the Holy Cross media dean Daniel Asara told Deseret News that believing powerful hidden actors control world events can create contradictions with core religious teachings, like trusting in God's providence. Hess notes that suspicion of "secret combinations" has deep roots in Latter-day Saint scripture, and cites Rutgers scholar Jack Z. Bratich and Boise State researchers on how the "conspiracy theorist" label itself can be misused to dismiss legitimate concerns. The piece argues that while seeking broader explanations for confusing events is natural, all-encompassing conspiratorial thinking can turn spirituality into something obsessive or defensive rather than a genuine motivating force.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess

item.title: More Salt Lake Temple open house tickets dropping in 2 upcoming waves
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced two more waves of ticket releases, on Sept. 15 and Oct. 1, for the public to tour the renovated Salt Lake Temple ahead of its 2027 open house. President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the Quorum of the Twelve told a press event inside the temple that leaders are "reaching out to all the world" to invite visitors, after the first 1 million tickets were claimed within 24 hours; church and civic leaders expect 4 to 5 million total visitors during the six-month celebration. The open house, themed "Rejoice in Christ," runs April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027, and will mark the first public access to the temple's interior in 134 years, featuring exhibits, performances and films. Tickets are available through TempleSquare.org or the Temple Square app, and a virtual tour option will be offered for those unable to travel to Salt Lake City.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Church News podcast: Hope in the modern dating landscape
item.description: In episode 311 of the Church News podcast, Brigham Young University marriage-preparation researcher Jason S. Carroll joins reporter Mary Richards to discuss findings from the National Dating Landscape Survey, a recent study showing only about one in three young U.S. adults are actively dating amid a broader decline in marriage and birth rates. Carroll, director of the Family Initiative at BYU's Wheatley Institute and a 20-year marriage-prep instructor, highlights "positive outlier" patterns from the research that he says point toward building a healthier dating and marriage culture. The episode is framed around teachings from Church President Dallin H. Oaks that family is central to Latter-day Saint doctrine, even as courtship trends shift nationally.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Tours underway for Idaho's newest Latter-day Saint temple
item.description: The Montpelier Idaho Temple opened for media tours Tuesday, with free public tours beginning Thursday, Sept. 10, and running through Sept. 26 (excluding Sundays) ahead of its Oct. 18 dedication. The temple, first announced by late church President Russell M. Nelson in April 2022 and under construction since June 2023, is a roughly 27,000-square-foot, two-story building on a 2.6-acre site featuring a chicory-flower motif and artwork by Kimbal Warren, Chris Manwaring, John Horejs and Josh Clare reflecting local wildflowers and nearby Bear Lake. It will become Idaho's eighth operating Latter-day Saint temple, serving the state's nearly 483,000 Latter-day Saints; Idaho currently has 11 temples announced, under construction or operating.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Embrace the awkward: It can create 'honor code-appropriate sparks,' BYU president tells students
item.description: BYU President Shane Reese urged students at the university's fall devotional to put down their phones and pursue in-person connection, telling them to "embrace the awkward" as a path to growth, dating and marriage. Reese cited data showing married BYU student rates have fallen to 17% from 25% in 2021, and shared stories of leaders who met their spouses by working up the courage to talk to someone waiting in line. He argued that friction and productive struggle, not frictionless scrolling through social media, build discernment, character and relationships, warning that letting artificial intelligence think or write for students won't develop their intellect or social skills. Reese framed Jesus Christ's outward focus on people like Zacchaeus as a model for turning attention away from screens.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Why these nuns are determined to build the impossible
item.description: A community of Discalced Carmelite sisters in Fairfield, Pennsylvania is building a monastery they hope will "last a thousand years," aiming to raise $100 million using traditional stone masonry, timber framing and reclaimed materials sourced locally, according to Deseret News religion writer Mariya Manzhos. The cloistered sisters, who follow a charism inspired by St. Teresa of Ávila, envision a self-sustaining, homestead-like community where they'll raise animals and spin wool. When the sisters struggled to find stonemasons willing to take on the old-world techniques they wanted, they called contractors from the phone book until they found Arch Masonry's Joe Bonifate, who said he immediately embraced the unconventional vision. Manzhos frames the project within a broader reflection on the meaning of work, citing Pope Leo's recent encyclical on labor as a source of identity and community, not just income.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: Elder Gilbert testifies of Christ in his first apostolic visit to West Africa
item.description: Elder Clark G. Gilbert of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is growing at "an amazing pace" in the Africa West Area, according to Church News. Gilbert made the comments in a social-media video during his first apostolic ministry trip to the region, spending Aug. 21-29 in Ghana and Sierra Leone alongside his wife, Sister Christine Gilbert. During the visit he ministered to local members and church leaders, framing the region's rapid growth as part of preparations for the Second Coming. The item notes readers can find Church News' full report at TheChurchNews.com.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Cathedral Church of St. Mark welcomes all to worship in Salt Lake City
item.description: The Episcopal Cathedral Church of St. Mark traces its Salt Lake City congregation back to 1867, when Bishop Daniel S. Tuttle arrived as a missionary bishop and members began meeting as St. Mark's Mission, according to cathedral historiographer Kurt Cook. Construction began in 1870, and the building notably reused sandstone blocks that Latter-day Saint workers originally cut for the Salt Lake Temple's foundation before switching to granite quarried from Little Cottonwood Canyon. The cathedral has been expanded several times since, including transepts added in the early 1900s, and survived both a 1935 fire and Utah's 2020 earthquake with only limited damage, though Cook said leaching in the old sandstone will eventually require costly repairs. Cook said the building remains well cared for more than 150 years after its bell first rang out over the city.
item.dc:creator: Joe Wirthlin

item.title: Opinion: The schedule for worship in the Church of Jesus Christ has always changed. Our need for belonging has not
item.description: In an opinion piece, content creator Jasmin Rappleye traces roughly 200 years of change in Latter-day Saint Sunday worship, noting the church's first 1830 sacrament service fell on a Tuesday and that early meetings were held in homes with communal cups, adult-administered ordinances and no fixed structure. She writes that individual sacrament cups only became common after 1911 and spread further during the 1918 flu pandemic, a shift some members resisted as it weakened the shared cup's symbolism of unity, a tension Rappleye compares to debates over hygiene practices during COVID-19. She also recounts how now-familiar organizations like Relief Society (1842), Sunday School (1849) and Primary (1878) began as grassroots efforts before becoming formal parts of Sunday worship over subsequent decades. Rappleye frames the newly split 25-minute second-hour classes, which began this week, as another entry in a long pattern of adaptation rather than a break from tradition.
item.dc:creator: Jasmin Rappleye

item.title: September Friend magazine focuses on the temple
item.description: The September 2026 issue of the Church of Jesus Christ's children's magazine, The Friend, is devoted to teaching children about temples, according to Church News. The issue, already reaching member homes and available online, explains why temples matter and how children of any age can begin preparing to attend, alongside content on what happens inside temples. The magazine's introduction emphasizes that temples are sacred spaces for learning about Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ and making covenants, and states that "Heavenly Father wants everyone to come to the temple." The item points readers to TheChurchNews.com for the full report.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Elder Soares ministers in Mexico, inviting thousands to center lives on Jesus Christ
item.description: Elder Ulisses Soares of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles invited more than 1,000 members at a special stake conference in Mexico on Aug. 30 to center their lives on Jesus Christ, especially during trials, according to Church News. The visit was part of a broader four-day ministry trip from Aug. 27-30, during which Soares also met with missionaries, journalists, religious leaders and government officials focused on dialogue, shared values and service, per the church's Mexico Newsroom. Soares quoted Doctrine and Covenants 6:36 in urging members not to fear as they build their faith. The item directs readers to TheChurchNews.com for further details.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: 5 ways to make the most of new Latter-day Saint Sunday meeting schedule
item.description: As Latter-day Saints began implementing the church's revised Sunday meeting schedule on Sept. 6, Deseret News' Amy Ortiz compiled guidance from church leaders on how members can get the most out of the change, which was first announced March 30. Elders David A. Bednar and Patrick Kearon emphasized that sacrament meeting, still capped at 60 minutes, should be about spiritual renewal rather than simply attending a meeting, urging members to let the experience of singing and worship be "transformed." Elder Bednar also stressed that individual members bear responsibility for their own gospel study rather than relying solely on the institutional church. Sunday School General President Paul V. Johnson said the new home-centered, church-supported model is meant to let members discuss at church what they've studied at home, with Young Women and Young Men general presidents likewise highlighting the value of daily personal study in a recent Church News podcast episode.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: What to know about applying for Church Educational System schools
item.description: Representatives from all six Church Educational System institutions — BYU, BYU-Idaho, BYU-Hawaii, BYU-Pathway Worldwide, Ensign College and Seminaries and Institutes — answered questions from prospective students and parents during a Sept. 1 livestream event, according to Church News. Panelists addressed whether a college degree is still worthwhile and how young adults can choose the right institution and prepare for the transition. Highlights included BYU-Pathway's global accessibility, BYU's academic and research strength, BYU-Hawaii's international mission, and Ensign College's career-focused training, alongside the spiritual grounding offered through seminary and institute programs. The item points readers to TheChurchNews.com for the complete recap.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ launches million-dollar initiative with UNICEF to aid mothers and children in South Asia
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and UNICEF launched a two-year initiative aiming to improve maternal and newborn health care for roughly 3 million mothers and infants across South Asia, with the church contributing $1.2 million specifically toward Pakistan, which has one of the world's highest neonatal mortality rates. Elder Kelly R. Johnson of the church's Asia Area Presidency said the effort builds on a long-standing partnership with UNICEF to help vulnerable mothers and children, while UNICEF's Sanjay Wijesekera noted that nearly two-thirds of under-five deaths in South Asia occur within a baby's first month of life. The initiative will fund medical supplies and equipment, train health workers to manage high-risk pregnancies and complications, and improve data systems, implemented in coordination with national and local health authorities. Relief Society General President Camille N. Johnson said the collaboration helps close resource gaps so families can feel more confident in the care they receive.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: A virtual Salt Lake Temple open house tour is coming. Here's what we can show you
item.description: Deseret News religion writer Tad Walch reported that The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is preparing a technology-rich virtual tour of the Salt Lake Temple so people worldwide can experience the 2027 Salt Lake Temple Celebration open house even if they can't travel to Utah. President Dieter F. Uchtdorf mentioned during Tuesday's news conference that some virtual video assets will be available as early as next month, while Elder Gary E. Stevenson said in a church social media post that the celebration "is not just for those who live nearby" but a worldwide event. The full virtual tour, expected to launch next April alongside the in-person open house, will use advanced 3D scanning technology captured by Johnny Rodriguez of Fresh Consulting, who used a specialized portal camera to capture "point clouds" inside the new Temple Square Visitors' Center that will let viewers explore spaces like the Celestial Room from any angle. The report comes as the first 1 million free in-person reservations for the six-month celebration, running April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027, sold out within hours of their release.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: 5 ways to prepare for the new youth Sunday experience
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is rolling out a new youth Sunday experience beginning Sept. 6, featuring shorter class times and a discussion-based curriculum alongside a revised "For the Strength of Youth" guide. Young Women General President Emily Belle Freeman and Young Men General President Timothy L. Farnes discussed the changes in a Church News podcast interview, explaining how youth, leaders and parents can prepare for the transition. Freeman said the updated approach is meant to equip and empower youth to live and share the gospel as part of preparing the world for the Second Coming of Jesus Christ. The story was reported by Church News, a Deseret-affiliated publication covering church news.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Elder Cook teaches missionaries 3 'keystones of faith' to anchor each testimony
item.description: Elder Quentin L. Cook of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles told missionaries at the Provo Missionary Training Center about a pivotal choice his older brother, Joe Cook, once faced between medical school and serving a full-time mission for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Cook recounted that the brothers agreed the decision should hinge on three questions he later called "keystones of faith": whether Jesus Christ is divine, whether the Book of Mormon is the word of God, and whether Joseph Smith is the prophet of the Restoration. Because the brothers answered yes to all three, they concluded a mission couldn't wait, even for medical school. Cook shared the story to encourage missionaries to root their own testimonies in those same three keystones.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: 1 million reservations: America’s hottest ticket is the Salt Lake Temple Celebration
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints says the first 1 million free reservations for the 2027 Salt Lake Temple Celebration open house were claimed within hours of their release Tuesday, with a quarter-million booked in the first 30 minutes alone. The reservations mark the first opportunity for general public tours inside the Salt Lake Temple since 1893, following its seven-year renovation, and church and civic leaders expect 4 to 5 million visitors during the six-month celebration running April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027. President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, acting president of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, and Utah Gov. Spencer Cox both spoke at Tuesday's kickoff event about the temple's historic and spiritual significance. Additional reservation batches for later months are still to come for those who missed this week's release.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Church leaders offer reasons you should be 1 of 5 million to tour the Salt Lake Temple next year
item.description: Church leaders including President Dieter F. Uchtdorf and Utah Gov. Spencer Cox spoke Tuesday at a kickoff event explaining why members of the public should reserve tours of the Salt Lake Temple during its 2027 open house, the first time the public has been allowed inside since 1893. Uchtdorf, acting president of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, said he hopes visitors arrive curious about why the church invested years renovating the pioneer-era temple, tying the answer to the celebration's theme, “Rejoice in Christ,” and Latter-day Saint beliefs about temples as literal houses of the Lord. Primary General President Rosemary K. Chibota and church historian Matt Grow also spoke, with Grow recounting the reported visit of Jesus Christ to the church's first temple in Kirtland, Ohio. Reservations for the roughly 5 million expected visitors began release Tuesday and sold out quickly, with more batches to follow for the tours running April 5 through Oct. 1.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: How should Christians think about AI?
item.description: Deseret News religion writer Mariya Manzhos reports on an AI summit in Nashville where representatives of the Episcopal, Evangelical Lutheran, Presbyterian and United Methodist churches — together representing more than 44,000 congregations — discussed how artificial intelligence is reshaping spiritual practice and formation. Evangelical Lutheran Church in America's Jace Martinez argued churches must remain “places of friction” where slow, effortful engagement with faith cannot simply be outsourced to AI tools. Attendees, including Anthropic spiritual director Chloe Lubinski, also discussed a July letter signed by more than 1,300 AI industry figures — including representatives from Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google — urging the U.S. government to help pace frontier AI development. The piece also describes individual attendees' uses of AI, from a pastor building simple apps for youth trips to a man creating an AI avatar to comfort his wife, who has dementia.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: This faith-based organization declined foreign government funding
item.description: Franklin Graham's Samaritan's Purse has declined a $300 million U.S. State Department grant for disaster response, part of the Trump administration's nearly $2 billion initiative directing foreign aid funding toward faith-based organizations. Graham said in an Aug. 28 statement that after prayer and discussion the organization withdrew as a recipient, saying it has “always relied on God, not government, for funding.” The State Department had named Samaritan's Purse alongside World Vision and Compassion International as partners in the effort, which aims to route $1.4 billion toward faith- and community-based health facilities and $538 million toward humanitarian response reaching 7 million people. Humanitarian aid experts told Deseret News the shift toward faith-based groups could leverage deep community networks but also raised concerns about all selected organizations being Christian, with consultant Abby Stoddard arguing aid decisions should rest on delivery capability rather than religious identity.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: 2026 youth music experiences resources now available
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has released resources for local wards and areas to plan their own in-person youth music experiences by the end of 2026, now available in English at youth.ChurchofJesusChrist.org under a “2026 Youth Theme Resources” tile, with other languages expected to follow. The brief Church News item, republished by Deseret News, notes there are three format options units can choose from to bring youth together in worship and celebration of their faith. The item directs readers to TheChurchNews.com for the full story and further details on the options.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: 'Rejoice in Christ' -- Salt Lake Temple Celebration theme is announced
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced Tuesday that "Rejoice in Christ" will be the theme of next year's Salt Lake Temple Celebration, unveiled by President Dieter F. Uchtdorf during the first public event held in the temple's new west entrance building. The celebration, running April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027, marks the end of a seven-year renovation and will offer the general public its first chance in the temple's 134-year history to tour the pioneer-era building, with free but reservation-required tickets released starting Sept. 1 at 11 a.m. MDT via TempleSquare.org and the Temple Square app. Elder Dale G. Renlund said the celebration's new experiences are designed to help visitors "learn of Jesus Christ," and Temple Square will offer exhibitions, performances and volunteer opportunities open to anyone 16 or older, including non-members. After the open house, the temple will be rededicated and reopened for regular temple worship.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Harmer, Tad Walch

item.title: Church wins unanimous federal ruling in tithing case appeal
item.description: A unanimous three-judge panel of the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Monday for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, upholding a 2025 district court dismissal of a consolidated class-action lawsuit in which nine plaintiffs sought the return of tithing donations made over roughly 25 years. Judges Harris Hartz, Gregory Phillips and Nancy Moritz found no reversible error in Judge Robert J. Shelby's ruling that the plaintiffs' fraud and misuse claims were filed after the three-year statute of limitations had expired, dismissing the case with prejudice. The panel avoided ruling directly on the broader church-autonomy doctrine that both sides had hoped to see addressed, a pattern also seen in the earlier Huntsman and Gaddy tithing cases; BYU law professor Gene Schaerr, who filed a brief on behalf of ten religious groups, called the outcome still a meaningful win for keeping courts out of churches' internal spending decisions. Church spokesman Sam Penrod reiterated that tithing funds are "carefully used and wisely managed" under church leaders' direction.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ opens doors to the Ephraim Utah Temple
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints opened the new Ephraim Utah Temple to media and invited guests Monday, ahead of a public open house running Wednesday through Sept. 19 and dedication by Elder Ronald A. Rasband of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. The temple, standing about 10 miles from the historic Manti Utah Temple, is the second in Sanpete County and was announced by President Russell M. Nelson in May 2021 after he said he received guidance to preserve the Manti temple's pioneer craftsmanship during its renovation and build a new temple in Ephraim instead. Nelson, whose mother was born in Ephraim and whose father was born in Manti, had noted at the 2022 groundbreaking that all four of his grandparents and all eight great-grandparents lived in Ephraim, immigrant converts from England, Denmark, Norway and Sweden. Utah is now home to more than 2.2 million Latter-day Saints and 32 temples that are operating, under construction, under renovation or announced.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Jane Weaver

item.title: Ground broken for Latter-day Saint temple in Coeur d'Alene, Idaho
item.description: Elder Hutch U. Fale, a General Authority Seventy of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, dedicated the site of the Coeur d'Alene Idaho Temple on Aug. 29, ahead of construction beginning on the new north Idaho temple. In his dedicatory prayer, Fale asked that the temple further the church's work, provide access to sacred ordinances for people on both sides of the veil, and stand as a symbol of peace for the surrounding Coeur d'Alene community. The brief announcement, credited to Church News, offers few additional construction details and points readers to TheChurchNews.com for the full story.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Latter-day Saint apostle dedicates Phnom Penh Cambodia Temple, where vision 'draws heavenward'
item.description: Elder Patrick Kearon of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles dedicated the Phnom Penh Cambodia Temple on Sunday, the 222nd operating temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, telling members the building's architecture and covenants are meant to draw their gaze and hearts heavenward. Kearon noted Cambodia's history of pain from the 1970s Khmer Rouge genocide, which claimed relatives of many Cambodian Latter-day Saints, and said the temple offers a place to exchange sorrow for peace; his wife, Sister Jennifer Kearon, called the temple a gift that lets Cambodians reach the presence of God without traveling to Hong Kong or the Philippines as members previously had to. The temple, announced in 2018 by President Russell M. Nelson and broken ground in 2021, sits on a 3.2-acre site along Russian Federation Boulevard and rises about 115 feet, with membership in Cambodia having grown from a handful of converts three decades ago to more than 18,000. Phnom Penh Cambodia North Stake President Samnang Sea, who helped coordinate the open house and dedication with the Cambodian government, said the temple will make members "strong and ready to be the light of the world."
item.dc:creator: Mary Richards

item.title: 3 Utah teens represent Team USA at world ultimate championships
item.description: Three Utah teens who are members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints -- Blake Holt of Hyde Park, Silas Bell of Logan and Emilee Jensen of Bountiful -- won medals representing Team USA at the World Flying Disc Federation's World Junior Ultimate Championships in Logrono, Spain, in July. Holt, 17, took silver with the U20 men's team, while Bell, 19, and Jensen, then 18, won gold on the U20 mixed team. Jensen is returning to Spain on a mission call to Madrid, and both Holt and Bell plan to serve missions after finishing high school.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Latter-day Saint apostle shares his own struggle with overachievement
item.description: Elder Patrick Kearon of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles told a crowd of more than 15,000 at BYU's Education Week devotional that he struggles with the same overachievement he was warning against, cautioning that tying self-worth to goals and productivity can crowd out the peace Christ offers. He cited research on excessive goal-setting showing that measuring every goal can reduce the joy of achieving it, and recalled being told by the late President M. Russell Ballard to "slow down" via a video message after over-reporting on an assignment. Kearon urged listeners to protect Sabbath rest despite demanding callings -- noting apostles themselves travel 40-plus weekends a year -- and said quiet contemplation, not further striving, is how people receive Christ's peace. He told the audience their best is good enough regardless of what they accomplish.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch
